articleTitle: Fetal heart monitoring by SQUID magnetometry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: The author has successfully carried out fetal magnetocardiographic studies using a Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) magnetometer. The technique, which is completely non-invasive and does not even require physical contact with the subject, is based on the detection of the magnetic fields generated by cardiac activity. Because magnetic fields are unaffected by changes in the electrical conductivity of the medium, measurement of the fetal magnetocardiogram (FMCG) may well prove not only simpler but more useful than the fetal electrocardiogram (FECG). The FMCG has been studied in a small group of normal subjects with the gestational age ranging from 28 to 35 weeks. In contrast to the FECG, the measured signal is completely uncontaminated by the maternal signal. The QRS complex is clearly visible in all cases and can be used for accurate beat-to-beat interval measurement. Further details of the fetal heart waveform, including the P-wave, can also be obtained by signal averaging.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: The new field of brain magnetic measurement is likely to make a major contribution to the understanding of brain function during the next decade. Results to date from scalp measurements show that it is possible to locate cortical activity to within 1-2 mm and magnetic activity in the depth of the brain to within 5-7 mm. Early results show that epileptic discharges can be satisfactorily monitored by this method, as can evoked potentials.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Visually evoked response measurements with a multi-channel magnetometer system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: The author has compared the topography of the visual evoked magnetic response to pattern onset stimuli and pattern reversal stimuli in four normal subjects. The topography of the magnetic equivalent of the CII component of pattern onset stimulation was compared with the P100 component of pattern reversal stimulation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Current developments in SQUID systems-low T/sub c/ and high T/sub c/-and their application to biomagnetism
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: Ever since SQUIDs (Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices) were used to demonstrate magnetocardiography in 1969, the promises of biomagnetism have been among the primary forces propelling the technology forward. Recent years have seen continuing advances, with further reductions in device noise, novel approaches to gradiometry, integration of SQUIDS with thin film pick-up coils, and further increases in the number of channels in commercial systems. Perhaps most significant, there have been very rapid developments in SQUIDs based on HTS (high temperature superconductors), which are now showing that they will have a major role to play in several aspects of biomagnetism. The authors briefly survey some of this progress.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Clinical measurements in multiple sclerosis with single channel magnetoencephalography
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: The authors have been assessing the clinical usefulness of a single channel MEG system, located within a 'cheap' eddy-current shielded room alongside a busy hospital Clinical Neurophysiology department serving a population of 2.7 million people with the emphasis not on the accuracy of resolution of a dipole source but rather on the other known properties of MEG compared with EEG namely the rejection of activity from distant sources, and the absence of the 'reference' problem. The comparison has therefore been between concurrently recorded conventional Evoked Potentials (EP) and magnetic evoked fields (EF).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Measurement of slowly changing magnetic sources in the brain
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: Slowly changing magnetic sources in the brain, rising and falling with a time course of minutes, have been associated with major pathological disturbances of ion concentrations in Spreading Depression. The authors describe progress and issues that arise in the application to human subjects of a technique devised to improve the resolution of such very low frequency (0.001-0.1 Hz) MEG recordings. It would be of value to obtain improved records from patients with concussion, stroke, and migraine. Slow signals may also occur in normal subjects.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Biomagnetic measurements in a clinical environment (slow wave activity)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: When analyzing spontaneous pathological focal activity the main problem is that the recorded signals are not only produced by the sources of interest. Thus, new tools had to be developed. These are the dipole-density-plot (DDP) with the approach to use the single dipole model only during adequate time sections and the current density localization obtained by spatial filtering.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: Magnetic field tomography studies have shown that with modern multichannel instruments it is possible to produce estimates of brain activity a few milliseconds apart and separate out neighbouring but distinct brain regions. It is nowadays feasible to study brain dynamics and its many parallel processes by non-invasive, non-contact measurements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of high temperature superconductors for shields and pick-up coils
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Biomagnetic Methods in Medicine
abstract: The authors focus on two applications of the new materials which are particularly relevant to biomagnetism in medicine and these are superconducting electromagnetic shields and superconducting pick-up coils for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). First, it is important to understand how the materials and devices which are the subject of discussion, are made and what effect the key properties, in particular the flux noise, have on the performance. These property investigations can often dictate which superconducting material offers a performance advantage.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
